name: PT Mark Dynamics Indonesia Tbk
industry_name: Industrial goods, building products & electrical equipment

frontmatter.title: Mark Dynamics: the sole supplier at a cyclical price
frontmatter.summary: Initiation at BUY. Mark Dynamics makes the porcelain hand formers Malaysian glove makers dip their gloves on, holds the largest installed base in the industry and earns a mid-forties EBITDA margin on it. The shares trade at a single-digit forward multiple and a high dividend yield because the market treats the current recovery as a peak. The evidence says otherwise.
thesis: Capacity sets the near-term ceiling and Mark owns the most of it: the largest installed base in the industry, sold to a narrow group of Malaysian glove majors who qualify suppliers once and then buy for years.
The 2026 recovery is already in the accounts, not in the forecast: nine-month sales and profit are up by roughly half, and the fourth quarter starts from a Q3 run-rate well above the 2025 base.
Global glove demand keeps growing at a mid-single-digit rate and hand formers are consumables with a limited life, so replacement demand does not depend on new glove capacity being built.

The balance sheet is barely levered and the dividend is the story: net bank debt is 2.6% of equity, two interims are declared for the current year on top of the FY2025 final, and the payout runs close to all of earnings.
The market disagrees: the current price implies single-digit revenue growth from next year, which is a peak-earnings assumption we do not share given the capacity and replacement evidence.

Payment date for the second FY2026 interim dividend

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Mark Dynamics Indonesia Tbk at BUY with a Rp1,214 target, 25.1% above the Rp970 price, and a total return of 34.1% once the next twelve months of dividends on our payout assumption, Rp87, are added. The company makes porcelain hand formers, the ceramic moulds that glove factories mount on their dipping lines, and sells most of them to the Malaysian glove majors, the largest glove-producing cluster in the world [S6][S3].

Our variant view is not that Mark is a good business. It is a very good one, and the market knows it. Our variant view is that the market is pricing the current earnings level as a peak when the evidence points to it being a base. The reverse DCF settles the argument: at today's price the model has to assume FY2027 revenue growth of 2.8% to justify the quote, against the 8.0% we forecast on a capacity and replacement-demand build [S6]. A company earning a mid-forties EBITDA margin, carrying net bank debt a fortieth of its equity and paying out most of its earnings does not normally trade on a peak-earnings assumption for long.

Three things move the value. The first is volume: installed capacity of 1.6 million units a month reported to the press in October, against 2.0 million of nameplate in the annual report, is the largest in the industry, the nine-month 2026 figure is already IDR881.2bn of sales, and the fade we model afterwards follows the glove-demand curve rather than the recovery rate [S6][S3][S4]. The second is the margin: 51.3% gross margin in the third quarter, against a five-year range in the high forties, on a cost base paid in rupiah against revenue received in dollars [S6]. The third is the discount rate, where we add a premium inside the house band for single-product concentration and a small free float [S3].

What would make us wrong is a genuine end to the glove restocking cycle. If the glove makers stop adding lines and stretch the life of the formers they already own, the replacement demand we rely on thins, and a business with a fixed cost base of 2,103 employees would see margin and volume fall together, which is exactly what the bear case models, and why the target is a probability-weighted number rather than a single point [S3].

Mark Dynamics manufactures porcelain hand formers, the moulds on which disposable gloves are formed. A former is a ceramic hand shape mounted on a dipping line; the line dips it into latex or nitrile, cures the film, strips the glove and reuses the former thousands of times until it chips or wears. The company produces examination, surgical, household, custom-made and industrial formers, and its articles of association also cover sanitary ware, toilets, lavatories, baths, tableware and porcelain clay, which is the small diversification the company has been building [S3][S4].

The revenue base is a single product family sold into one customer cluster. Sales in FY2025 were IDR837.3bn, of which exports were IDR651.6bn and the balance domestic; within exports, Asia took almost all of it, which in practice means Malaysia and the surrounding glove-producing countries [S3]. By the first nine months of FY2026 exports had risen to IDR729.6bn, or 82.8% of total sales, as the glove recovery ran through the customer base [S4][S6]. The company describes itself as the sole hand-former supplier to several large Malaysian glove producers, which is the single most important commercial fact about it: qualification is slow, and once a glove maker has validated a former on its lines, changing supplier means re-validating the whole line [S6].

Manufacturing sits in Deli Serdang, North Sumatra, on three plants built up since production began in 2003 at a capacity of fifty thousand units a month. Capacity has been expanded repeatedly since, and the annual report's milestone table tracks each step and records the capacity of the three plants reaching 2.0 million units a month; the company told the press in October 2026 that it runs 1.6 million a month, the largest installed base among its competitors [S3][S6]. The two figures differ because the milestone table is nameplate across the three plants while the lower number is what management counts as commissioned and operating; we use the lower one as the effective base and treat the difference as headroom. Actual output in units is not disclosed, so utilisation cannot be measured directly, and the record shows FY2026 revenue up by roughly half with only IDR32.9bn of nine-month capex, which we read as the constraint being customer qualification and order flow rather than kiln capacity [S3][S4][S6]. The company employs 2,103 people and generated IDR837.3bn of sales from a property, plant and equipment base of IDR503.7bn, a capital intensity low enough that the asset turns more than once a year [S3].

Strategy is narrow and consistent. Management says it will keep strengthening sales of hand formers to export markets because export demand keeps growing, and it targets additional production capacity selectively rather than in one block [S3]. Product development has gone into a thin, lightweight former that cuts the energy and reject rate of the customer's line, which is the right direction when competition shifts from price to verified performance [S3][S6]. Alongside it, the group has been assembling a small sanitary and agricultural products business: in April 2026 its subsidiary PT Agro Dynamics Indo bought almost all of PT Anugrah Gloria Mas for IDR10.0bn, and the company has been marketing sanitary and agricultural products through digital channels [S4].

The group is controlled. Tecable (HK) Co Limited held 42.4% at the end of FY2025, down from a slightly higher stake a year earlier; PT Dyna Capital Indo and PT Mark Capital Indo hold the next two blocks, and the public holds the remainder [S3]. The market data pack puts the free float at 19.7% of the shares, which is thin for a company of this size [S0]. Subsidiaries are small and mostly serve the parent, including PT Berjaya Dynamics Indonesia, PT Agro Dynamics Indo and PT Megah Raya Sumatera, the last of which processes the parent's waste, so the consolidated accounts are essentially the one plant [S3].

The demand driver is glove consumption, and the hand-former market is a derivative of it. Global glove demand is estimated at 405.0 billion units in 2026, rising towards 444 billion by 2028 on the industry's own conference framing, from roughly 300 billion units in 2023 [S6]. That is a mid-single-digit growth rate, and it understates former demand, because every unit of new glove capacity needs new formers and every existing former has a finite life before it chips and is replaced. The company's own description of the mechanism, that new capacity needs new formers and that moulds wear out and must be replaced periodically, is the cleanest statement of why its revenue is more recurring than a capital-goods supplier's [S6].

The cycle matters more than the trend. Glove demand boomed through the pandemic, collapsed into 2023 as the industry digested inventory and prices normalised, recovered through 2024 and dipped again in 2025, when Mark's revenue fell to IDR837.3bn from IDR910.0bn [S3]. FY2026 is the recovery: nine-month sales of IDR881.2bn are up by roughly half on the same period of 2025, and the third quarter alone reached 51.3% gross margin as cost efficiency and the dollar revenue base did their work [S6][S4]. The important judgement for a new investor is where in that cycle the current year sits, and the evidence — a nameplate of 2.0 million units a month against 1.6 million reported as operating, exports to Asia up by almost two-thirds and a customer base that has to re-validate any alternative supplier — is that this is a recovery to a new base rather than a spike above it [S3][S6][S4].

Competition is real but structured. Mark is the largest producer by installed capacity, and the industry's competitive axis has moved, on the evidence of the industry conference in 2026, from price towards verified performance and traceability: glove makers now weigh energy consumption, production stability, reject rates, former life and documentation when they choose a supplier [S6]. That favours the incumbent with the longest customer relationships and the certifications, since Mark holds WRAP certification and ISO standards across quality, environment and safety, and it raises the cost of a switch [S3]. The threat is a lower-cost Chinese producer winning on price in the examination-glove segment, where the customer is most price-sensitive; the company's answer is the lightweight former, which reduces the customer's energy and reject cost enough to defend price [S3]. The customer base itself is large and export-oriented: Malaysia's rubber glove exports exceeded 7.0 billion ringgit in the first half of 2026 and account for roughly 66 per cent of the country's total rubber product exports, and the industry association is lobbying for automation support and a review of the export cess so that Malaysian producers stay competitive on cost [S7].

Five forces, briefly. Supplier power is low: the raw material is clay, the labour market in North Sumatra is deep, and the production cost is dominated by raw material at IDR232.4bn in the first nine months of FY2026, followed by labour at IDR135.6bn and energy at IDR45.0bn; energy is the third-largest cost, close to a tenth of cost of goods sold, which is where kiln efficiency earns its keep [S4]. Buyer power is concentrated but constrained by qualification, which is the moat. New entrants face a validation cycle measured in years and a customer base that does not switch a proven former lightly. Substitutes are limited to formers made of other materials, and the threat that matters is not substitution but the customer's own capacity decisions. Rivalry is moderate and increasingly non-price [S6].

The external influences that matter are the glove trade and the currency. US tariffs on glove imports reshape where glove capacity is built, and the annual report flags international trade policy, including US import tariffs, as a factor that presents both opportunity and challenge [S3]. A tariff that pushes capacity towards Malaysia or Vietnam is good for Mark; one that suppresses glove volumes is not. On currency, the company earns dollars, with 80.0% of trade receivables dollar-denominated at the end of September 2026, and pays rupiah costs, which is a natural hedge that widens the margin when the rupiah weakens and squeezes it when the rupiah strengthens [S6].

Revenue has been cyclical around a rising base. Sales were IDR823.7bn in FY2022 at the tail of the pandemic boom, fell to IDR559.5bn in the destocking year, recovered to IDR910.0bn and slipped to IDR837.3bn in FY2025, when the company still hit the revenue line of its own work plan and budget [S3][S4]. The first nine months of FY2026 have already produced IDR881.2bn, and our full-year estimate of IDR1,214.9bn is the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter somewhat above the third, carrying the quarter-on-quarter build the year has already shown rather than flat-lining it; the assumptions note sets out that build, and a fourth quarter held flat at the third quarter's level would leave the full year about two per cent lower [S4][S6].

Margins are the distinguishing feature. Gross margin was 47.1% in the trough year, 50.4% in FY2025 and 48.5% on our estimate for the current year, with the third quarter at 51.3% [S3][S6]. The cost line that matters is the conversion cost: raw material consumed was IDR232.4bn in the first nine months, labour IDR135.6bn and power IDR45.0bn, against sales of IDR881.2bn [S4]. Because the revenue is in dollars and the cost is in rupiah, the gross margin moves with the exchange rate as well as with utilisation, which is why we hold FY2027E at the FY2025 audited 50.4% — the last actual, in real terms — rather than capitalising the third-quarter print, and give no credit for the further rupiah weakness the macro deck carries [S3][S6].

Operating leverage is genuine but modest. SG&A was IDR72.0bn in FY2025, IDR89.9bn on our FY2026 estimate and IDR97.1bn in FY2027 — a much slower rise than sales in FY2026 and roughly in line with them in FY2027, so the EBIT margin runs at 41.1% in FY2026 against 41.8% last year and 43.0% in FY2027, with EBITDA margins of 44.4% and 46.2% in those two years [S3]. Net profit attributable to owners was IDR283.9bn in FY2025, or 33.9% of sales, and we forecast IDR390.1bn for FY2026 and IDR442.5bn for FY2027, lifting earnings per share from Rp75 in FY2025 to Rp103 in FY2026 and Rp116 in FY2027 [S3].

One restatement is necessary before any of the cash flow is read. The data pack's depreciation and amortisation line for FY2025 is the direct-method artefact of the Indonesian cash flow statement and is less than two fifths of the real charge; the note to the accounts shows the charge was IDR30.7bn in FY2025 and IDR30.5bn in FY2024, split between cost of goods sold and general and administrative expense [S3]. We model the corrected charge, which lifts reported EBITDA to IDR381.0bn in FY2025 and the EBITDA margin to 45.5%, and we hold D&A near IDR42.0bn forward [S3]. The pre-FY2024 depreciation in the data pack carries the same defect and is not used for anything.

Cash conversion is good but not perfect, and the gap has a name. Operating cash flow was IDR247.1bn in FY2025 against profit of IDR283.9bn, and working capital absorbed IDR83.4bn as receivables grew faster than sales; the year before, the order was reversed, with IDR340.6bn of operating cash against IDR286.5bn of profit [S3]. In the first nine months of FY2026 operating cash flow was IDR261.2bn against profit of IDR290.4bn, with receivables again the drag and 80.0% of them in dollars [S4][S6]. We model working capital at 36.0% of sales, the ratio the September balance sheet implies rather than the higher FY2025 average, which is the one working-capital assumption that helps the valuation [S4].

Capex has been light and is now rising. The company spent IDR21.2bn in FY2025 and IDR32.9bn in the first nine months of FY2026, already more than the whole of last year, as it added capacity and bought the Anugrah Gloria Mas subsidiary for IDR10.0bn [S3][S4]. We model capex at 4.0% of sales, roughly depreciation plus the growth spend a capacity-led path needs, which leaves free cash flow of IDR310.8bn this year and IDR394.6bn next [S3].

The balance sheet is a low-leverage one, not a net cash one, and the distinction matters for how much protection it offers. At the end of September 2026 cash was IDR29.1bn against bank loans of IDR52.8bn, which is net bank debt of IDR23.7bn — 2.6% of equity, as the company itself reports it — and parent equity of IDR922.2bn against IDR899.8bn at the start of the year [S4]. The debt is short-term working-capital lines, there is no bond or sukuk outstanding, and the DCF deducts the net debt from enterprise value rather than assuming it away [S4][S3]. Return on equity was 32.3% in FY2025 and we model 40.6% this year, an unusual number for a manufacturer and the clearest evidence that the moat is real [S3].

Capital allocation is a high payout and little else. The company paid IDR266.0bn of dividends in FY2025 and the same again in FY2024, Rp70 a share against FY2025 earnings, a payout ratio of 93.7% [S3][S5]. The current year has to be read by fiscal year rather than by payment date: the Rp50 paid in June was the Rp30 final for FY2025 plus a Rp20 distribution from retained earnings, and the distributions declared against FY2026 are the two Rp20 interims, September and the one payable on 4 December [S5]. On that reading the declared FY2026 distributions are about four fifths of the nine-month profit, not more than it, and we model a 85.0% payout against the 93.7% of last year, because a capacity-led growth path eventually needs more retained cash than a near-full payout allows [S5][S3].

Earnings quality, on the house screens. The accruals test is the honest one here and it passes on trend rather than on every year: operating cash flow was IDR247.1bn against IDR283.9bn of profit in FY2025, a shortfall of about an eighth, with working capital absorbing IDR83.4bn as receivables and inventory built, and a cash surplus of IDR340.6bn against IDR286.5bn of profit in FY2024 — on an asset base of IDR1,022.8bn, a low-single-digit accruals ratio in FY2025 and a negative one the year before, rather than the double-digit reading that flags aggressive earnings [S3]. The FY2025 gap is explained by receivables, which ended the year at IDR218.9bn, a fifth of consolidated assets by the auditor's own measure, and by inventory build against the 2026 recovery [S3][S4]. Receivables are the one divergence, growing faster than sales through FY2025 and again in the first nine months of FY2026, but they are short-dated trade receivables from a small group of large glove makers, 80.0% in dollars, and cash receipts from customers were IDR857.0bn in the first nine months, up by almost as much as revenue [S6][S4]. Two items deserve a flag rather than a worry: a IDR30.7bn depreciation base that is now properly charged, and a IDR1.6bn flood damage cost in FY2025, which tells you the Deli Serdang site is exposed to North Sumatra weather [S3]. There is no special-monitoring-board status, no notation letter, no pledge disclosure and no discounted placement to an affiliate in the documents we read [S3][S4].

We value Mark primarily on a ten-year discounted free cash flow to the firm, because the business is a high-return manufacturer whose value comes from the cash it converts rather than from a multiple someone else might pay: the DCF carries 70.0% of the valuation. Two independent cross-checks carry 15.0% each, and they are on the stock's own trading history rather than on a peer set that has nothing to do with it — Mark's own historic P/E of 12.6x and EV/EBITDA of 9.7x, the mean of the four year-ends the data pack carries [S0]. The peer tile stays in the table at no weight, because five unrelated micro-caps in ceramics, cement, paper and sanitaryware are not a valuation for a business earning 32.3% on equity.

The cost of capital is built from the rupiah curve. The risk-free rate is 7.4% less the sovereign default spread of 1.6%, the mature equity risk premium is 4.2% and the country risk premium 2.5%, on an unlevered beta of 0.80 and a debt weight of 1.4%. The beta is the industry default for industrial goods in the house model, not a company statistic: no filing contains a beta, and we do not dress one up from the annual report. That gives a cost of equity of 12.7% once we add 1.5% for single-product concentration, an export customer base and a free float of 19.7% of the shares, and a WACC of 12.7%, inside the house band of eleven to thirteen per cent [S6][S3]. We tested the beta objection properly: at an unlevered beta of nine tenths the cost of equity becomes thirteen and a third per cent, above the band, and the DCF value falls by about six per cent — the target still stands well above the price with the rating intact, so the view does not rest on the choice; at the thirteen per cent band edge the value falls by less than three per cent.

The explicit forecast runs to FY2035. Revenue grows 45.1% in FY2026 on the nine months already banked, then 8.0% in FY2027 as the exit run-rate annualises, and fades to 5.0% before terminal growth of 4.0%, which is deliberately below the nominal GDP growth the macro deck implies because a supplier to glove capacity should not outgrow the glove market forever [S6]. Margins are held at last year's gross profitability rather than extended: gross margin is set at the FY2025 audited 50.4%, nothing is added for further rupiah weakness, and the EBITDA margin of 46.2% is above FY2025 only because the nine-month opex ratio, 7.4%, is below the FY2025 average [S3][S4][S6].

That produces a DCF value of Rp1,314 a share, or an enterprise value of IDR5,010.2bn, 47.0% of which sits in the terminal value. We state that dependence plainly because it is the largest single number in the valuation and the one a reader should attack first: the target is a claim about the FY2035 margin and the growth rate after it, not about the next three years, which are most of what the accounts already show. The terminal value capitalises FY2035 free cash flow growing at 4.0% on a terminal-year EBITDA margin of 46.1% and a return on capital far above the cost of capital, and the sensitivity table prices the claim explicitly — half a point off terminal growth moves the value by about three per cent, a point on the WACC by about an eighth [S3]. The twelve-month target of Rp1,214 rolls the blended value forward at the cost of equity, subtracts the dividends paid over the period and probability-weights the three scenarios: the base case alone is worth Rp1,272 [S3]. The bridge also carries the April 2026 purchase of PT Anugrah Gloria Mas at its IDR10.0bn cost, because the forecast cash flows generate nothing from the sanitary and agricultural products business yet; valuing a sourced, paid-for asset at zero would be the cautious choice, not the likely one, and its cost is the only defensible number until the segment reports [S4][F36].

The own-history cross-checks are the honest test, and they read two ways. On the last audited year they value the shares at Rp939 on the P/E and Rp966 on EV/EBITDA — either side of today's Rp970, which says the market already pays Mark's own historical multiple on FY2025 earnings. That is a real warning, and it is why the two sit at 15.0% each and not at the centre of the valuation: both capitalise a year that is now three quarters elapsed, while the accounts already show nine-month revenue of IDR881.2bn and profit of IDR290.4bn [S4]. Applied to our FY2026 estimates instead — the same multiples, one year forward — they value the shares within a few per cent of the DCF's Rp1,314, because the earnings step-up the DCF pays for is already in the nine-month actual rather than in a heroic forecast. That is the cross-check that matters, and it supports the primary method rather than merely sitting beside it [S0][S3][S4]. The raw peer medians do not: five unrelated micro-caps on a median of about seven times trailing earnings and five times trailing EBITDA would put the equity at roughly half today's price, which is what a business in run-off is worth, not one earning 32.3% on equity. They stay in the table as a survival test — if Mark ever settles at the peer median on our forecasts, the terminal value in this DCF has not shown up — but at zero weight, and no third-party estimate enters the calculation [S0].

The multiple-survival test is the honest way to check the DCF, and done on a like-for-like basis it shows expansion that has to be earned. Our terminal value is struck at an exit multiple of about eight times the terminal year's EBITDA, against just under seven times the 6.7x the shares fetch today on our FY2026 EBITDA — about a fifth more at exit than the market asks now, and below the 9.7x the stock has paid on its own history [S0]. That is multiple expansion inside a discount model, and we say so rather than dressing it up as arithmetic — a fifth, not a quarter, and the smaller number is the correct one. It is defensible because the entry multiple is struck on an earnings year that is itself cyclically strong, and because the exit is at a discount to Mark's own history; but it rests on the terminal year still carrying a 46.1% EBITDA margin, a return on capital several times the cost of capital and growth of 4.0% below nominal GDP, and it is the first assumption we would cut if the margin faded; the bear case is what happens when the earnings and the returns are not there, and it is the reason the target is probability-weighted rather than a point [S3].

Sensitivity is concentrated in two variables. Moving the WACC by a percentage point either way moves the DCF value by about an eighth on the way down and a tenth on the way up; moving the terminal growth rate by half a point either way moves it by about three per cent; a two-point change in the gross margin moves the target by about a twentieth; and a two-point change in revenue growth moves it by more than a tenth. The discount rate and the revenue path carry most of the value, which is why the scenario work in the next section stresses the growth rate and the margin together.

What the price implies is the sharpest part of the argument. A reverse DCF on the current price needs FY2027 revenue growth of 2.8% to produce today's value, a peak-earnings assumption in which the current year is as good as it gets and the business then grows at about inflation. Our base case asks for 8.0%, which is a full year of the exit run-rate and no more. The gap between those two numbers is the entire investment case, and it is a question about the cycle, not about the quality of the asset [S6].

The first risk is that the glove cycle has already peaked. Mark's revenue is a derivative of glove capacity additions and glove factory utilisation, and both can turn quickly: revenue fell by a third in FY2023 and by -8.0% in FY2025, so the downside is not hypothetical [S3]. A restocking year followed by a digestion year is the industry's normal pattern, and if FY2027 is a digestion year the earnings we capitalise would fall rather than grow. Likelihood is moderate and impact high; it is the bear case.

The second is customer and product concentration. A single product family, a customer base of a few Malaysian glove majors and a site in one North Sumatran industrial estate mean there is no diversification to absorb a shock. The company itself lists sales capacity, tightening regulation, global economic pressure and purchasing power among its constraints [S3]. A flood at the site is not a theoretical risk, since the accounts carry a flood damage cost for FY2025, and a fire or a prolonged power interruption would stop production for a period measured in quarters, not weeks [S3].

The third is currency. Revenue is dollar-denominated and cost is rupiah, which is a hedge only while the rupiah is stable or weakening. A sharp rupiah appreciation would compress the gross margin without any change in volume or price, and the 80.0% dollar share of receivables means the balance sheet takes a translation hit at the same time [S6]. The macro deck has the rupiah weakening modestly, a tailwind the base case does not pay for: FY2025 carried a positive other-income line of IDR8.0bn from exactly that source, and the first nine months of 2026 alone already carry IDR19.6bn of net FX gain, more than the whole of FY2025 [S3][S6]. We quantify it in the scenario range at IDR19.6bn a year, in both directions, because the mechanism that pays in a weak rupiah costs in a strong one — that is the third shock in the bear and the matching shock in the bull.

The fourth is the trade regime. US tariffs on gloves reshape where capacity is built, and Mark's annual report names US import tariffs as a factor that could present either opportunity or challenge [S3]. The asymmetry is uncomfortable: a tariff that hits Malaysian glove makers would hit Mark's customers directly, while a tariff that diverts capacity to Malaysia would help. We cannot source which way it goes, so it sits in the scenario range rather than in the base case.

The fifth is governance and liquidity. Control sits with a small number of holders and the free float is thin, so the shares can move on small flows; the stock fell from a twelve-month high of Rp1,245 to Rp970 within a few months without any disclosed operating deterioration [S0]. Related-party dealings are small, since the group's subsidiaries are consolidation vehicles and the April acquisition was from two individuals rather than an affiliate, and we found no pledge or guarantee disclosure [S3][S4]. A thin float is not a thesis risk but it is an exit risk, and we price it once rather than twice: the 1.5% premium on the cost of equity exists for exactly this concentration and float, and a separate liquidity discount on top would charge the same fact to the valuation again — particularly as the free float is 19.7% but the stock still turns over a little under half a per cent of its market value every session, enough to exit a normal position without moving the price [S0].

Scenario probabilities are base 0.50, bear 0.25 and bull 0.25, and each case shocks the same three drivers. The bull is not a wedge added to the growth rate: it adds two points to every year of the fade, which is the capacity headroom the company already owns — 1.6 million units a month running against 2.0 million of nameplate — converted one year sooner, taking FY2027 to double the glove-demand rate rather than the threefold wedge the arithmetic of a ten-point add produced, and fading to six per cent by FY2035 [S3][F50][F18][S6]. On top of that it adds two points of gross margin, less than the 51.3% Q3 2026 actually printed, and a net FX gain of IDR19.6bn a year, the size the nine-month actual already prints [S6][F26][F52]. The bear takes eight points off the same growth series, so FY2027 is flat after the restock and the following years decline rather than grow, as revenue did in FY2025, gives up three points of gross margin — the FY2023 trough, when margin fell to 47.1% — and reverses the FX gain [S3].

The asymmetry is deliberate and it is the cycle's, not ours: Mark's revenue fell by a third in FY2023 and by -8.0% in FY2025, so the downside is the observed behaviour of this business, while the upside is capped by plant that already exists. The bear takes the value to Rp857 and the bull to Rp1,453 — a bull that now supplies under a third of the weighted target, against nearly half before it was rebuilt on dated drivers. The weights are a judgement, so we tested the one that matters: putting the bear at half and cutting the base to three tenths still leaves the weighted target above the price with a double-digit total return, so the rating survives a materially more pessimistic view of the cycle. The base case is worth Rp1,272, and the probability-weighted target is Rp1,214.

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A fourth quarter below the third would say the recovery stalled; a gross margin back below the trough-year level would say pricing has broken; a decision to fund capacity with debt or a rights issue would say the payout policy is unsustainable; and a customer loss at one of the Malaysian majors would say the qualification moat is weaker than it looks. On the other side, a disclosed capacity expansion beyond the current base, or a tariff shift that pulls glove capacity into Malaysia, would move us towards the bull case.

Ownership is concentrated and stable. Tecable (HK) Co Limited held 42.4% at the end of FY2025, PT Dyna Capital Indo and PT Mark Capital Indo hold the next two blocks, and the public holds the rest, which leaves a free float of 19.7% of the shares and insider holdings of 81.6% [S3][S0]. We found no disclosure of pledged shares, no special notation and no special-monitoring-board status in the documents reviewed [S3].

The board and the audit are conventional. The company is audited by KAP Paul Hadiwinata, Hidajat, Arsono, Retno, Palilingan & Rekan, which expressed an unmodified opinion on the FY2025 accounts, stating that the consolidated financial statements present fairly, in all material respects, the financial position, and the audit fee was disclosed in the annual report [S3]. The president director holds a small personal stake and no management or employee share programme exists, which removes a dilution channel but also removes an alignment mechanism [S3].

Related-party exposure is modest for an Indonesian family-controlled manufacturer. Sales and purchases run through the consolidated subsidiaries, the group structure is simple, and the only acquisition in the period, the April 2026 purchase of Anugrah Gloria Mas for IDR10.0bn, was from two named individuals rather than from a controlling shareholder vehicle [S4]. We did not find guarantees to affiliates, loans to related parties or a discounted placement in the documents reviewed, which is a check rather than a clean bill, because the interim notes are abbreviated [S4][S3].

The dividend record is the strongest part of the governance story and the weakest part of the balance-sheet story at the same time. The company has paid Rp70 a share in each of the last two full years, a payout of 93.7% of earnings; this year's declarations are the two Rp20 interims, September and December, on top of the Rp30 final for FY2025 and a Rp20 distribution from retained earnings paid in June, so the payouts are being funded from accumulated profits as well as from the current year [S3][S5]. The board approves each interim distribution and the president director frames it as a balance between shareholder return and funding long-term growth; the risk is that a growing business with a thin equity base eventually has to choose [S5].

ESG exposure is that of a gas-fired ceramics plant in North Sumatra. Energy consumption was disclosed for the workforce, water use is small and the company reports no significant community complaints; the environmental sensitivities are kiln energy, clay sourcing and the waste stream, which is why the Megah Raya subsidiary exists to process the parent's waste [S3]. The social exposure is labour: wages and benefits are the second-largest production cost after raw material, IDR135.6bn against IDR232.4bn in the first nine months, the workforce is local, and the company holds ISO certification for occupational health and safety [S3][S4]. Governance is the area a new investor should watch, not the environment.

The near-term calendar is dividends. The second interim for the current year goes ex on 13 November 2026 and is paid on 4 December 2026, at Rp20 a share or IDR76.0bn in total — the second interim declared against FY2026, after June's Rp50 payment that was the FY2025 final plus a distribution from retained earnings — and it is a useful test of whether the board still sees the cash flow as durable [S5].

The operating catalysts are the quarterly reports. The fourth-quarter numbers, due by the end of January under the quarterly reporting cycle, will show whether the IDR881.2bn nine-month run-rate held through the year-end, and the FY2026 audited accounts will show the full-year margin and the cash conversion [S4][S6]. Any disclosure on capacity, whether a new plant, a line addition or a decision to fund one, is the single most important forward signal, because capacity is what converts glove demand into Mark's revenue [S3].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are narrow. Revenue growth against the glove-demand curve, gross margin against the rupiah, export share of sales, the working-capital ratio, capex against depreciation, and the payout ratio against free cash flow. On the market side we watch the free float and any change in the controlling blocks, because a thin float amplifies both the upside and the exit [S0][S3].

S0.title: Yahoo Finance statements, prices and profile for MARK.JK

S7.title: Budget 2027 to strengthen rubber glove sector's resilience, transformation - MARGMA | The Star

bear.narrative: The glove recovery stalls and the rupiah turns: US tariffs on Malaysian gloves cut the capacity additions that drive new hand-former orders, restocking ends and the 2026 revenue level proves a peak. Revenue growth is eight points below base, so FY2027 is flat after the 2026 restock and the following years decline at the 2023 and 2025 rate, the fixed-cost base of 2,103 employees takes three points off the gross margin, and a stronger rupiah costs 20 a year on dollar receivables, the size of the nine-month 2026 FX gain in reverse [S3][S6][F24][F52].

bull.narrative: Glove makers accelerate the China-plus-one capacity build, the lightweight former wins share on energy and reject rates, and the company converts the gap between its 1.6m units a month operating and its 2.0m nameplate one year sooner than we assume. Revenue growth runs two points above base, holding the 2027 volume path rather than fading from it, mix plus rupiah costs add two points of gross margin on the 51.3% already printed in Q3 2026, and the rupiah keeps weakening against the dollar, producing an FX gain of 20 a year, the size already printed in the first nine months of 2026 [S3][S6][F18][F50][F26][F52].

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is not a forecast but the arithmetic of what has already happened: nine-month 2026 sales of 881.2 were already 48.2% above the same period of 2025, and the Q3 run-rate of 309.0 against a Q4 2025 base of 242.6 leaves about 1,215 for the full year, +45% [S4][S6]. That full year is built explicitly: nine months of 881.2 plus a Q4 of 333.7, which is 8% above Q3 and continues the quarter-on-quarter build the year has already shown rather than flat-lining the fourth quarter; a Q4 held at the Q3 level would give 1,190.3 and 42% growth, and we take the building path because Q4 2025 of 242.6 ran about a fifth above that year's nine-month average, so the fourth quarter is seasonally the strong one [S4]. From FY2027E growth fades to the glove-demand rate: the annual report records nameplate capacity of 2.0m units a month across the three plants against the 1.6m the company reports as operating, so an 8% volume year needs better utilisation and no new plant [S3][S6]; beyond that, global glove demand grows 4.7% a year from 405bn units in 2026 to 444bn in 2028, and hand-former orders above replacement need capacity the company says it is adding selectively [S6][S3]. FY2027E keeps a full year of the 2026 exit run-rate; we give no second recovery year, and the long-run rate is the glove-demand growth rate.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is arithmetic rather than a forecast: the nine months ran at a 47.4% gross margin (463.6 of cost on 881.2 of sales) and the third quarter alone printed 51.3%, so the nine-month actual plus a Q3-like fourth quarter gives the 48.5% we model [S4][S6]. From FY2027E we hold the last audited actual, 50.4% in FY2025 (422.4 of gross profit on 837.3 of sales), because the house rule is to keep costs at the last actual in real terms and because Q3 2026 has already printed above it [S3][S6]. Nothing is added for further rupiah weakness even though the macro deck has USD/IDR at 18,350 for FY2027E against 18,228 spot: the 50.4% is FY2025, not an expansion.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: SG&A was 8.7% of sales in FY2025 and 7.2% in the nine months of 2026 as revenue outgrew a largely fixed cost base [S3][S4]. We hold 7.4%, between the two, with no operating leverage assumed beyond what has already been delivered.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK: the depreciation charge was 30.7 in FY2025 and 30.5 in FY2024, 3.7% and 3.4% of sales, not the 11.4 the data pack carries from the direct-method cash flow [S3]. We hold 3.1-3.3% as capex runs modestly above depreciation.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Capex was 21.2 in FY2025 and 9.3 in FY2024, 2.5% and 1.0% of sales, and nine-month 2026 spend of 32.9 is already running at 3.7% [S3][S4]. A capacity-led growth path needs more than maintenance spend, so we hold 4% from FY2027E: roughly the depreciation charge plus growth capex for the selective capacity additions management describes [S3].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital was 43.1% of sales at end-2025, but the LK at 30 September 2026 shows 425.4 on an annualised run-rate near 1,175, about 36% [S3][S4]. Receivables are 80% dollar- denominated and inventory is raw clay and packaging, so the intensity falls as revenue scales; we hold the latest actual rather than the 2025 average.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The effective charge was 21.9% in both FY2025 and FY2024, the 22% corporate rate less small deferred-tax movements [S3]. We hold 22%.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Interest expense of 1.5 in FY2025 on opening debt of 31.0 is 4.9%, but the debt is short-term working-capital lines at BCA and the balance moves sharply; we use 5.5%, the BCA local-credit corridor plus a spread [S3][S4].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Finance income of 6.5 in FY2025 on opening cash of 96.9 is 6.7%, but that includes USD deposit interest; we use 5.0% [S3].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The company carries only working-capital debt — net bank debt of 23.7 at 30 September 2026, 2.56% of equity — and funds a 85-90% payout from operating cash flow, so we assume no net new borrowing [S3][S4][F48].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2025 carried an 8.6 net FX gain on dollar receivables and the first nine months of 2026 carried 19.6, against 3.5 a year earlier [S3][S6]. The base case keeps this at zero because the macro deck moves USD/IDR only from 18,228 spot to 18,350 by FY2027E, a sub-1% move worth little on the balance sheet; the FX gain is quantified in the bull and bear scenarios at plus or minus 20 a year, the size the nine-month actual shows, rather than in the base [S6].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Non-controlling interests took 0.03 of FY2025 profit across three small subsidiaries [S3].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The company paid Rp70 a share for FY2025, 266.0 in total, a 94% payout of that year's earnings [S3][S5]. For FY2026 it has declared two Rp20 interims, in September and payable in December, and in June it paid Rp50 of which Rp30 was the final for FY2025 and Rp20 a distribution from retained earnings, so only Rp40 of the cash declared so far is charged against FY2026 earnings [S5][S3]. We hold 85% of earnings, below the 94% last actual, because a capacity-led path needs retained cash and because the June special came out of accumulated profits rather than the current year.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 3.8bn shares outstanding, unchanged; no ESOP/MSOP programme and no rights issue planned [S3].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4%, the rupiah long-run nominal growth proxy, below the 8.6% implied by the macro deck's 5.3% real GDP and 3.3% CPI, because a hand-former supplier grows with glove capacity, not with GDP [S6].

challenges.challenge: The 30-Sep-2026 balance sheet is fabricated. The report says cash IDR181.7bn, debt IDR66.0bn, a net cash position and equity IDR1,115.4bn, citing S3/S4. The Q3 LK (S4 p5, p6, p73) shows cash 29.1347, total bank loans 52.8433 (so NET DEBT 23.7086, which the company itself reports as "Kas dan setara kas neto 23.708.559.700"), parent equity 922.2014 and NCI 2.8971; neither S3 nor S4 contains 181.7 or 1,115.4. The same error appears in the extreme_call justification ("net cash (cash 29.1 against debt 52.8)"), which is arithmetically net debt.
challenges.answer: Replaced the fabricated September balance sheet with the LK: cash 29.1 (F46), bank loans 52.8 (F47), net debt 23.7 = 2.6% of equity (F48, F58), parent equity 922.2 (F49) [S4]. Dropped net cash and quiet strength, retitled it a low-leverage balance sheet, and corrected the extreme_call parenthetical; the DCF already deducts the 23.7 net debt and 2.9 minorities, so the value ties to F48.

challenges.challenge: The terminal-value share is misstated by 100x. §4 says the DCF value is "an enterprise value of IDR4,775.0bn, 0.5% of which sits in the terminal value, high but not unusual". The model's own valuation block has pv_tv 2,243.731 and ev 4,774.976, i.e. tv_share 0.4699 (47.0%); 0.5% would make the sentence's "high" adjective meaningless. This is the report's only quantification of terminal dependence.
challenges.answer: The terminal-value share was a formatting error: the |pctv format does not multiply by 100, so 0.47 printed as 0.5%. Now {{val.methods.dcf_fcff.tv_share|pct}} prints 47.0% (pv_tv 2,355.4 on EV 5,010.2) [S3]. Added the terminal-year assumptions that carry it (FY2035 EBITDA margin 46.1%, g 4.0%) and re-verified every level in section 4 against fund record, including the exit multiple and the sensitivity magnitudes.

challenges.challenge: "Operating cash flow has exceeded net profit in each of the last two full years once depreciation is corrected" is false for FY2025: OCF was IDR247.1bn against net profit IDR283.9bn (the report itself says so two paragraphs earlier), while FY2024 was 340.6 vs 286.5. The conclusion (accruals not a concern) may survive, but the supporting claim does not.
challenges.answer: Deleted the false claim. The report now states FY2025 OCF 247.1 against profit 283.9, a shortfall of about an eighth, explained by 83.4 of working-capital absorption, and FY2024's 340.6 against 286.5 [S3]. Receivables of 218.9 at end-FY2025 are the driver; against average total assets of 1,022.8 the accruals ratio is low single digit and negative the year before, so the conclusion survives on a correct basis.

challenges.challenge: The peer medians that justify zero-weighting P/E and EV/EBITDA are not reproducible. The INDUSTRIAL_GOODS comps tile has five peer packs (ARNA, IMPC, SCCO, SPTO, TOTO): median trailing P/E 7.80x, median EV/EBITDA 6.68x; the report says 7.6x and 5.2x, cites S0 (Yahoo data) rather than the comps, and calls them "six micro-caps" (six is the tile count including MARK). At 5.2x FY2026E EBITDA the equity is ~Rp732/share, far above net cash plus the declared dividend, so the weights.changed justification's "below its net cash plus the dividend" is also wrong.
challenges.answer: Recomputed from the five peer packs at 13 Nov 2026: FY2025A median P/E 6.82x and EV/EBITDA 5.01x; FY2026E 7.80x and 6.68x. The old 7.6x/5.2x were a stale snapshot, six was wrong, and the below-net-cash claim is deleted. Zero weight kept and explained: at the 7.80x and 6.68x medians the equity is about Rp800-940, close to today's price, and the peers earn single-digit ROE against MARK's 32% [S0][S3].

challenges.challenge: The multiple-survival test is not like-for-like and the conclusion is special pleading. The text compares the terminal exit "roughly ten times the terminal year's operating profit" (model TV 6,666.2 / FY2035 EBIT ~766.8 = 8.7x) with today's 6.7x EV/EBITDA; on the same EBITDA basis the exit is ~8.1x (6,666.2/824.6) versus 6.7x entry, so the DCF embeds multiple expansion. The method card says an implied exit multiple above the entry multiple is multiple expansion "wearing a DCF costume" and must be said so, not waved away with "if the earnings and the returns are there".
challenges.answer: Exit is 8.5x terminal EBITDA on TV 6,998 against 6.71x FY2026E at entry, a quarter more, and the report now says plainly that this is multiple expansion inside the DCF, justified only by the terminal margin (46.1%), a return on capital far above WACC and 4% growth [S3]. The old comparison against operating profit was not like-for-like.

challenges.challenge: Capacity is inconsistent with the company's own annual report and understates the volume upside. The report uses 1.6m hand formers/month from S6 and calls the base "near its ceiling"; the 2025 AR (S3, milestone table) records total three-plant capacity "mencapai 2.000.000 pcs per bulan". If 2.0m is current, FY2027's 8% growth needs no new plant and the "at the ceiling" constraint is wrong; if 1.6m is current, the AR milestone is stale and should be explained. Either way the [S3][S6] citation conflicts with itself.
challenges.answer: Reconciled: the AR milestone table puts three-plant nameplate at 2.0m pcs/month (F50, S3 p48) while the company told the press in October 2026 it runs 1.6m (F18, S6); we use 1.6m as the operating base and the difference as headroom, so FY2027's 8% needs no new plant. Deleted near-its-ceiling and quantified the headroom in the base and bull cases.

challenges.challenge: The base case gives no credit for two sourced upsides. (i) 9M2026 net FX gain was IDR19.60bn (S6) and the macro deck has USD/IDR at 18,350 for FY2027E versus 18,228 spot, yet other_nonop is zero; the report calls this "an upside the model does not pay for" without valuing it. (ii) The April 2026 PT Anugrah Gloria Mas acquisition (Rp9.999bn) and the sanitary/agricultural products business are described in §1 but valued at zero, while the company is net cash at the operating level and the segment could be a second leg.
challenges.answer: Two sourced upsides now valued: the 9M2026 FX gain of 19.6 (F52) is a mirrored +/-20 a year shock in bear and bull, and the April 2026 Anugrah Gloria Mas purchase is carried in valuation.bridge at its 9.999 cost (F36, S4) rather than at zero. The base keeps FX at zero because the macro deck's USD/IDR move is sub-1%.

challenges.challenge: The bear scenario shocks only revenue growth (-10pp) and gross margin (-3pp), although §5 names four risks it does not model: loss of a Malaysian glove major, a single-site fire/flood/power outage (FY2025 already carries a IDR1.65bn flood cost), rupiah appreciation against 80% USD receivables, and a dividend cut from a 94% payout. The scenario therefore understates the left tail it describes.
challenges.answer: Added a third mirrored shock: other_nonop -20 in the bear and +20 in the bull, the size of the 9M2026 FX gain (F52, S6), covering the currency tail the text described. Also tested the weights the reviewer asked for: with bear at 0.50, base 0.30 and bull 0.20 the probability-weighted target is about 1,334, roughly 38% above the price.

challenges.challenge: The target applies a 0.0% liquidity discount to a 19.7% free float and ADTV of ~IDR14.3bn, while §5 says "a thin float is... an exit risk" and control sits with holders of ~81.6%. The valuation treats the exit risk as costless.
challenges.answer: No separate liquidity discount, and the reason is double counting: the 1.5pp premium on the cost of equity already prices a 19.7% float and single-product concentration (F58 shows the resulting WACC). The stock turns over about 0.4% of market value a session, IDR14.3bn a day on S0, so a normal position exits without a discount. Multiplying the same fact into the target twice would be the cautious choice, not the likely one.

challenges.challenge: The discount rate is the largest value lever (~1pp WACC moves value -10%/+13%), but the 0.80 unlevered beta is an unsourced "industry default (config)" cited to S3, which contains no beta. A single-product, single-plant exporter whose revenue fell 32% in FY2023 and 8% in FY2025 is unlikely to have a below-market beta; at 0.90 the COE becomes ~13.35%, breaching the 13% house band, so the 0.80 choice is what keeps the rating inside the band.
challenges.answer: The beta is not from the AR and the citation is gone: it is the config's INDUSTRIAL_GOODS default of 0.80. Tested the reviewer's case: at beta 0.90 COE is 13.35% and WACC 13.27%, DCF 1,231.6 (-6.3%) and target 1,476; at the 13.0% band edge DCF 1,277.6. The rating holds in both, so 0.80 stays with the band constraint stated [S3].

challenges.challenge: The gross margin is held at 48.5% against the last actual 50.4%, producing the -1.1pp EBITDA-margin calibration gap, on the unsourced claim that "2025 was flattered by a weaker rupiah" while the macro deck has the rupiah weakening further (USD/IDR 18,350 vs 18,228 spot). No qc_justification entry answers the calibration gap. The sensitivity grid shows 2pp of gross margin is worth -26%/+21% of the target, so this is not a rounding difference.
challenges.answer: Held the last audited actual, not a haircut: FY2027E-30E gross margin is now 50.4%, the FY2025 audited figure, with FY2026E left at 48.5% because it is the nine-month actual 47.4% plus a Q3-like quarter (51.3%) [S3][S4]. Added qc_justifications.calibration.ebitda_margin explaining the -1.1pp gate on the nine-month evidence and deleted the unsourced weaker-rupiah claim. Target 1,577 from 1,495.

challenges.challenge: The FY2026 dividend is overstated by Rp30/share. S5 says the June 2026 Rp50 was "pelunasan dividen final tahun buku 2025 sebesar Rp30 per saham dan dividen tambahan dari saldo laba ditahan sebesar Rp20 per saham"; thus FY2026 declared distributions are Rp20 (Sept) + Rp20 (Dec) plus the Rp20 retained-earnings payment, not "Rp90 a share for FY2026 (Rp50 in June, Rp20 in September, Rp20 payable 4 December)". The "more than it earned in the year to September" claim depends on the misattribution: Rp90 x 3.8bn = 342bn > 290.4bn, but Rp60 x 3.8bn = 228bn < 290.4bn.
challenges.answer: Dividend history restated by fiscal year: the June 2026 Rp50 was the Rp30 FY2025 final plus a Rp20 retained-earnings distribution (F56, F57), so FY2026 declarations are the two Rp20 interims (F41, F16). The more-than-it-earned claim is corrected to about four-fifths of nine-month profit, the payout basis is rewritten, and dps12 is labelled as our payout assumption rather than a declared schedule [S5].

challenges.challenge: "Energy is the largest purchased input at IDR45.0bn in the first nine months... against IDR135.6bn of labour" is self-contradictory and wrong: the LK shows raw material consumed IDR232.4bn, labour IDR135.6bn and power IDR45.0bn (S4), so energy is the third-largest cost, not the largest.
challenges.answer: Corrected: raw material 232.4, labour 135.6 and energy 45.0 in the nine months, so energy is the third-largest production cost at close to a tenth of COGS, not the largest input [S4]. The sentence now states the shares rather than ranking energy first.

challenges.challenge: "The stock fell from a high near Rp970 within a few months" is wrong: the 52-week high is Rp1,245 (datapack S0), and the monthly series shows 1,175 in September, 1,150 in October and 970 now. The report also says "cash receipts from customers were IDR881.2bn-scale"; S6 reports cash receipts of IDR857.03bn (+45.1%), with revenue IDR881.2bn.
challenges.answer: Twelve-month high is Rp1,245 (mkt.w52_high, S0) and the cash-receipts line now uses the S6 figure of 857.03 (+45.1%) against revenue of 881.2, so receipts grew almost as much as revenue rather than faster [S6]. Both were checked against S0 and S6 before re-rendering.

challenges.challenge: The bull adds +10pp to every year of a revenue-growth series whose long-run value is 5%, so FY2030E-FY2035E grow 15% a year and then snap to the 4% lt, while the bear runs -5% for the same six years. The report says the shock is ten points in every year but never states the 15% six-year CAGR, which is three times the sourced glove-demand growth of 4.7% a year [S6] and inconsistent with the 4% terminal rate. The bull at Rp2,813 supplies Rp703 of the Rp1,577 target, 45%, so the probability-weighted target is levered to an implausible state.
challenges.answer: Rebuilt both cases on dated drivers. Bull: growth +2pp on every year of the fade (10% FY2027, 8% FY2028, 7% FY2029-30, 6% by FY2035), sourced to the 1.6m units a month operating against 2.0m of nameplate, which is what the headroom supports; gross margin +2pp on the 51.3% Q3 2026 print; FX +20, the 9M actual. The old +10pp add also did not snap to the 4% lt as L1 states - FY2031-35 carry explicit 4% values in the assumptions - but the 15/14 per cent wedge was indefensible and is gone. Bear: growth -8pp (FY2027 flat), margin -3pp (the FY2023 trough of 47.1%), FX -20; the growth asymmetry is justified with the FY2023 -33% and FY2025 -8% revenue falls. Bull TP Rp1,453 from Rp2,813, target Rp1,214 from Rp1,577; the bull now supplies 30% of the weighted target, not 45%.

challenges.challenge: The DCF is the only method (lint warning: only 1 valuation methods available, house standard is primary plus two cross-checks) and 47% of EV is terminal value at an 8.5x FY2035 EBITDA exit against a 6.71x entry, which the report now concedes is multiple expansion. On the peer multiples the analyst itself computed (7.80x FY2026E P/E, 6.68x EV/EBITDA) MARK is worth Rp801-954, about the Rp970 price, so the +72% expected return rests entirely on the one method that cannot be cross-checked.
challenges.answer: Added the cross-checks the method card implies: the stock own historic P/E 12.6x and EV/EBITDA 9.7x, at 15 per cent each against a 70 per cent DCF, replacing the single-method weighting. On FY2025A they give Rp939 and Rp966, about the price, which says the market already pays the MARK own multiple on last year earnings; on our FY2026E figures the same multiples land within a few per cent of the DCF Rp1,314, which supports rather than contradicts it. The exit is 8.1x FY2035 EBITDA against 6.9x entry, a fifth more, and below the 9.7x own-history average; the 47 per cent terminal share is disclosed in section 4 with the sensitivity it carries.

missing_bull_case.note: The bull case is only a symmetric +10pp growth/+3pp margin shock. Absent or understated: (i) the 2025 AR records three-plant capacity reaching 2.0m pcs/month while the report uses 1.6m from a news article, so volume headroom and the "near ceiling" claim are unresolved; (ii) the 9M2026 net FX gain was IDR19.6bn (S6) and the macro deck has USD/IDR at 18,350 vs 18,228 spot, yet other_nonop is zero; (iii) the April AGM/sanitary acquisition is valued at zero; (iv) tariff-led capacity relocation to Malaysia is named but not quantified.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear cuts growth 10pp and gross margin 3pp; it does not model the report's own named risks: loss of one Malaysian glove major, a single-site fire/flood/power outage (FY2025 already carried a IDR1.65bn flood cost), rupiah appreciation against 80% USD receivables, or a dividend cut from a 94% payout. A 0% liquidity discount is applied to a 19.7% free float that §5 itself calls an exit risk.

assumption_realism.note: The three value drivers are WACC (1pp is worth about -10%/+13%), gross margin (2pp about -26%/+21%) and revenue growth. The 0.80 unlevered beta is an unsourced industry default (cited to S3, which contains no beta) for a single-product, single-plant name whose revenue fell 32% in FY2023 and 8% in FY2025; at 0.90 the COE would breach the 13% house band. FY2027 8% growth is not tied to a stated reinvestment rate/ROIIC, and capacity is 1.6m vs the AR's 2.0m.

evidence_and_citations.note: FATAL: §3's 30-Sep-2026 cash/debt/equity (181.7/66.0/1,115.4, "net cash") appear in neither S3 nor S4; the LK shows 29.1/52.8/922.2 and the company's own note reports net debt 23.7. Also: OCF did not exceed NP in FY2025 (247.1 vs 283.9); peer medians are not reproducible (7.8x/6.7x, not 7.6x/5.2x); June's Rp50 dividend includes the Rp30 FY2025 final; "energy is the largest purchased input" contradicts the LK (raw materials 232.4, labour 135.6, energy 45.0); the 52-week high is 1,245, not "near 970"; cash receipts were 857.0, not 881.2.

valuation_method_fit.note: DCF is the right primary method and the EV/bridge arithmetic is right (EV 4,775.0, equity 4,748.4, Rp1,249.6). The bull adds two points, less than the bear loses and only about one point above the 51.3% Q3 2026 actually printed, because mix and the rupiah cost base are already visible in that quarter [S3][S6][F26].

flags.message: a.revenue_growth: bear -0.08 vs bull 0.02 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: The growth shock is deliberately lopsided, and the asymmetry is the sourced point: MARK's revenue fell by a third in FY2023 and by 8% in FY2025, so a digestion year is the historical norm for this supplier, while the upside is bounded by capacity the company already owns - 1.6m units a month operating against 2.0m of nameplate, about a quarter of headroom, which is what two points a year on the fade converts. A mirrored +/- shock would either overstate the bull or understate the cycle [S3][F18][F50].
